clue.text: Fine and kind of brill?

definitions.note: a definition by example, flagged by the question mark

indicators.note: 'and' simply adds the second piece after the first one here

blocks.note: F is the pencil-grading abbreviation for fine
the suffix -ish means sort of or kind of

explanation.surface: Someone praising a thing as fine and, in slang, brill, meaning brilliant.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface wants 'brill' as British slang for brilliant; it is really the flatfish, so the question mark flags an example.
explanation.definitionFit: Brill is a European flatfish closely related to turbot, so it is one example of the wider category.

clue.text: Divisive bit of info on debtor’s documents

indicators.note: in a down clue, one piece sitting on another places it above, so first

blocks.note: a fact is a single item of information
IOUs are written promises a debtor signs

explanation.surface: A snippet of information spotted in paperwork belonging to someone who owes money, causing division.
explanation.walkthrough: An IOU spells out 'I owe you', and the plural keeps its capital letters as IOUS.
explanation.definitionFit: Factious describes groups splitting into quarrelling factions, which is exactly what divisive behaviour produces.

clue.text: Unemotional criticism, mostly involving nothing

indicators.note: most of the word for criticism is used, so its last letter goes
the shortened criticism takes in 'nothing' as part of itself

blocks.note: stick is informal criticism, as in 'taking stick'; drop its final letter
O looks like a zero

explanation.surface: A cool, detached critique that mostly concerns nothing at all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stick' as criticism is British informal usage: to give someone stick is to mock or scold them.
explanation.definitionFit: A stoic endures hardship without showing feeling, named after the Greek philosophers who taught calm acceptance.

clue.text: Look to return with wine as a memento

indicators.note: returning sends the word for look back the way it came
'with' sets the wine alongside the first piece

blocks.note: to peek is to take a quick look
sake is Japanese rice wine

explanation.surface: Someone planning to go back with a bottle of wine as a souvenir of a trip.
explanation.walkthrough: The reversal applies only to the look word; the wine joins unchanged afterwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words name a small object kept to remind its owner of a person or occasion.

clue.text: One-time hoodlums regularly fleeing

definitions.note: a verbal noun standing for the noun

indicators.note: taking letters at a regular interval from 'hoodlums', every second one

blocks.note: ex- means former, as in ex-wife
the even-placed letters of hoodlums

explanation.surface: Former gang members making a run for it.
explanation.walkthrough: The selection keeps the second, fourth, sixth and eighth letters, skipping the initial H.
explanation.definitionFit: An exodus is a mass departure of people, a crowd leaving together, so fleeing captures the movement.

clue.text: Specialist insight given by Pacino for one acting

indicators.note: the insight is followed by what the actor supplies, adding the pieces in order

blocks.note: a pro is an expert
vision is foresight or insight
Al Pacino is one person called Al

explanation.surface: Expert wisdom shared by Al Pacino about a performer's craft.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface makes 'acting' about the stage, but it is the adjective for a temporary stand-in, as in acting manager.
explanation.definitionFit: Something provisional holds a role only for now until a permanent arrangement replaces it, like an acting chairman.

clue.text: Ordered a surprise attack over a radio

indicators.note: something broadcast over a radio is heard rather than read

blocks.note: a raid is a sudden attack

explanation.surface: A commander issuing orders for a surprise strike over the radio.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ordered' reads as a command being given, but it is the adjective meaning set out in order.
explanation.definitionFit: Troops or items that are arrayed have been drawn up and arranged in neat ranks or formation.

clue.text: Each street is right on the map

blocks.note: ea. is the standard abbreviation for each, as on price lists
St is the standard abbreviation for street

explanation.surface: Someone checking that every street is marked correctly on a map.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Right' looks like 'correct', but it means the right-hand side of a map.
explanation.definitionFit: Maps are conventionally drawn with north at the top, placing the eastern compass direction on the right-hand side.

clue.text: Chief technical officer about to come to grief, nearly

indicators.note: the officer's title goes around, or about, the phrase meaning to come to grief

blocks.note: the standard initials for this job title
to lose is to be defeated, to come off badly

explanation.surface: A company's tech chief on the verge of disaster.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface ties 'nearly' to coming to grief, but it stands alone as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Close to a number means almost reaching it, so the phrase works as an adverb of approximation.

clue.text: Perpetual movement of giant levers

indicators.note: the letters of 'giant levers' are moved about into a new order

blocks.note: the eleven letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Huge levers in endless motion, like a perpetual-motion machine.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface evokes perpetual motion; 'Perpetual' is actually the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe something that never ends and continues without stopping forever.

clue.text: Source of money taken away from old car plant

indicators.note: the source of a word is where it starts, its first letter
the initial of money is removed from the old car's name

blocks.note: the opening letter of money
Morris was a British car maker, famous for the Morris Minor

explanation.surface: A funding stream withdrawn from a disused car factory.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plant' reads as the factory, but it is the definition, a flower.
explanation.definitionFit: Orris is a kind of iris whose fragrant root is dried and used in perfumes.

clue.text: Disbelief is represented crudely in it

indicators.note: to be represented is to be presented again in a new form, rearranged

blocks.note: the eleven letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Scepticism being portrayed in a rough, clumsy way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crudely' looks like the anagram signal, but it is part of the fodder along with 'in it'.
explanation.definitionFit: Incredulity is the state of being unable or unwilling to believe something, a direct synonym.

clue.text: After ten years, a collection of books is deteriorating

indicators.note: the collection of books is placed after the period of ten years

blocks.note: a decade is ten years
NT, the New Testament, is a collection of books of the Bible

explanation.surface: A library going to ruin after a decade of neglect.
explanation.walkthrough: NT and OT are standard crossword shorthand for the two halves of the Bible, each a collection of books.
explanation.definitionFit: Decadent describes a society or culture in moral or cultural decline, sliding from former standards.

clue.text: In the end, you often discover you feel totally rebellious

indicators.note: taking the end of each of the following words

blocks.clueFragment: you often discover you feel totally
blocks.note: the final letter of each of the six words

explanation.surface: A reflective remark that, eventually, people find themselves completely defiant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In the end' reads as 'eventually', but it tells you to take the last letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Unruly people are disorderly and hard to control, resisting discipline much as rebels resist authority.

clue.text: Stop in a few bars?

blocks.note: a verb: to hold back from doing something
a recurring musical phrase or chorus

explanation.surface: Someone stopping off in several pubs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bars' suggests pubs, but these are bars of music; the question mark admits the pun.
explanation.definitionFit: A verb meaning abstain, and a noun for the repeated line or chorus of a song.

clue.text: Lied terribly to cover up extremely dim-witted swindle

indicators.note: 'Lied' is done badly, its letters thrown out of order
the extremes of 'dim-witted' are its outermost letters
the rearranged lie wraps around, or covers, the selected letters

blocks.note: the four letters to rearrange
the first and last letters

explanation.surface: A foolish con artist lying badly to hide a stupid scam.
explanation.walkthrough: The rearranged fodder splits after its second letter to take in the pair of Ds.
explanation.definitionFit: To diddle someone is informal British usage for cheating them out of money by trickery.

clue.text: Bottomless prosecco, possibly more than once — that’s great for everyone

indicators.note: in a down clue the bottom is the last letter, which is removed
the shortened drink is used again, set after itself

blocks.note: prosecco is an example of wine; drop its last letter
the same shortened drink repeated

explanation.surface: A bottomless-brunch deal where the prosecco keeps flowing, and everyone is happy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bottomless prosecco' is a brunch offer of unlimited refills; here it means the last letter comes off.
explanation.definitionFit: A win-win situation is one where every party involved gains and nobody loses anything.

clue.text: Drunk Oasis fan hit somebody with it?

indicators.note: drunk letters stagger out of their proper order

blocks.note: the eleven letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A drunk fan of the band Oasis hitting someone, perhaps with an object.
explanation.walkthrough: Oasis are a British rock band. 'With it' reads as a weapon, but it means fashionable.
explanation.definitionFit: Being 'with it' is dated slang for trendy, and a fashionista is devoted to following the latest styles.

clue.text: Standard part of a risotto recipe

blocks.note: an adjective: usual, regularly used, as in a routine reply
the broth that rice is cooked in

explanation.surface: A basic, standard element of a risotto recipe.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as one phrase, but 'Standard' is a complete definition on its own, an adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Stock means ordinary or routinely used, and it is also flavoured broth added gradually to risotto rice.

clue.text: Shady scheme requiring computers to be set up

indicators.note: in a down clue, set up means lifted so it reads bottom to top

blocks.note: Macs are Apple computers

explanation.surface: A dodgy plan that needs computers to be installed first.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Set up' reads as installing machines, but in a down clue it means turned upside down.
explanation.definitionFit: A scam is a dishonest scheme to cheat people, a fraud or racket.

clue.text: Animal seen in Morocco, at intervals

indicators.note: the answer can be seen inside the run of words that follows

blocks.note: moroCCO AT Intervals, spanning three words

explanation.surface: A creature spotted now and then in Morocco.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At intervals' looks like an alternate-letters instruction, but it only supplies letters for the hidden run.
explanation.definitionFit: The coati is a long-snouted raccoon relative from the Americas, a kind of mammal.

clue.text: We ultimately fail to show up for reception

indicators.note: ultimately points to what comes last in the word 'fail'

blocks.note: used as it stands
the final letter
to come is to arrive or turn up

explanation.surface: An apology for not turning up to a wedding reception.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fail to show up' reads as one phrase, but 'fail' supplies only its last letter and 'to show up' stands alone.
explanation.definitionFit: A welcome is the greeting given to arriving guests, just as a reception is how they are received.

clue.text: Guy getting on and leading the team

indicators.note: 'and' joins the second piece directly after the first

blocks.note: a guy is a man
getting on means growing old

explanation.surface: An older man still in charge of a sports team.
explanation.walkthrough: AGING is the American spelling; British English usually writes ageing.
explanation.definitionFit: Managing a side means running it and being in charge, as a football manager directs the players.

clue.text: Second gear required for take-off

blocks.note: s is the abbreviation for second
kit is equipment or clothing

explanation.surface: A second item of equipment needed before an aircraft can leave the ground.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Take-off' suggests a plane departing, but it means a parody or send-up.
explanation.definitionFit: A take-off is a comic imitation, and a skit is a short satirical sketch mocking something.
